warmup.q: Container client (10.10.1.10) has an empty ARP cache. It pings peer (10.10.1.20) on the same Docker network. How many ARP packets cross the wire before the first ping can leave?
options: None: the switch already knows which port 10.10.1.20 is on
One: client broadcasts a request, and peer starts answering pings
Two: a broadcast request from client, then a reply from peer sent only to client
Four: a request and a reply in each direction, so both sides learn each other
warmup.why: Client broadcasts who-has 10.10.1.20, and peer sends its reply to client's MAC alone. Peer doesn't need to ask back, because it learned client's MAC from the request itself. The switch can't answer for anyone: it knows MAC addresses, never IP addresses.

sections.h: Every card on a link needs a name: the MAC address
sections.html:
Lesson 1 of this track left one picture: a frame crosses one link at a time, and on each link a MAC address says which card should take it. This lesson zooms into that link layer. Start with the problem a MAC address solves.

On one link, every card can hear every transmission. The first Ethernet of the 1980s was literally one long coaxial cable that every computer clipped onto. Wi-Fi still works like that: every laptop in range receives every frame on its channel. So a card needs a way to tell "this frame is for me" from "this frame is for someone else". That means every card needs a name, and every frame must carry the name of the card it is for.

That name is the MAC address (media access control address): 48 bits, written as six bytes in hex, such as 2e:cb:30:15:a6:0f. Every frame starts with the destination MAC, then the source MAC. A card compares the destination with its own address and drops frames that don't match, in hardware, before your kernel ever sees them.

A name only works if no other card on the link has it. The simplest rule that guarantees this is to give every card ever made a different address, and that is how it started. The IEEE, the standards body behind Ethernet, sells each manufacturer a 3-byte prefix called an OUI (organizationally unique identifier), and the manufacturer numbers its cards with the other 3 bytes. 48 bits allow about 281 trillion addresses, so they won't run out.

That rule breaks as soon as software makes network cards. Docker creates a virtual card for every container, hypervisors create them for virtual machines, and nobody buys an OUI for that. So one bit of the first byte, the U/L bit (universal or local), says which kind an address is: 0 means a vendor assigned it, 1 means someone made it up. A made-up address only has to be unique on its own link, and a random number with 46 free bits almost always is. Phones and laptops make up addresses too when "private Wi-Fi address" is switched on, so a café's network can't recognise the same device on every visit.

One more need: some frames are for everybody. ARP, later in this lesson, has to ask every card on the link a question. So the lowest bit of the first byte, the I/G bit (individual or group), marks group addresses. 0 means one card. 1 means a group: a multicast address that several cards chose to listen to, or the all-ones broadcast address ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, which every card accepts.

So you can read any MAC from its first byte. 2e is 0010 1110 in binary. The lowest bit is 0, so it names one card. The next bit is 1, so it was made up: this is a Docker container, and Docker picks a new random address every time it starts one.

The rest of the frame is short. After the two addresses come 2 bytes of EtherType, the "what's inside" field from lesson 1 (0x0800 for IPv4, 0x0806 for ARP, 0x86dd for IPv6), then 46 to 1,500 bytes of payload, then a 4-byte checksum that the receiving card checks and strips off. A payload shorter than 46 bytes gets zero padding, which is why the lab in lesson 1 cut the IP packet at its own length field, not at the end of the frame.

try.title: Read your own MAC
steps: Start the lab box from the labs folder (docker compose -f env/labbox.yml run --rm box) and run the three lines below. The last one prints the two flag bits of the first byte.
Exit and start the box again, then rerun them. Predict first: same MAC, or a new one?
On your Mac, ifconfig en0 | grep ether prints the address Wi-Fi is using. If its second hex digit is 2, 6, a or e, the U/L bit is set: a private (made-up) address.

code.title: in the lab box
code.html: ip -br link show eth0 mac=$(cat /sys/class/net/eth0/address); echo $mac o=$((16#${mac:0:2})); echo "first octet $o I/G bit: $((o & 1)) U/L bit: $(((o >> 1) & 1))"

try.expect:
From one run:

eth0@if220       UP             2e:cb:30:15:a6:0f <BROADCAST,MULTICAST,UP,LOWER_UP>
2e:cb:30:15:a6:0f
first octet 46  I/G bit: 0  U/L bit: 1

I/G is 0 (one card) and U/L is 1 (made up). After a restart the MAC is different but the two bits are the same: Docker draws a new random, locally administered address every time it starts a container.

sections.h: A switch learns where each card is, so frames stop going everywhere
sections.html:
A shared cable has two problems that get worse with every computer you add. Only one card can transmit at a time, so a hundred computers share one cable's speed. And every card receives every frame, including frames full of other people's data.

The first improvement was the hub: a box with one socket per computer that copies every signal it receives out of all its other sockets. That makes the wiring tidier, but inside the box it is still one shared cable, with both problems.

A switch fixes both by learning. For every frame that comes in, it reads the source MAC and remembers which port the frame arrived on. (Linux's software switch keeps each of those memories for 300 seconds by default.) When a frame arrives for a destination it has learned, the switch sends it out of that one port only. Two pairs of computers can now talk at full speed at the same moment, and nobody else hears them.

What should the switch do with a frame for a MAC it hasn't learned yet, for example just after it starts? It can't know the right port, and dropping the frame would break the network. So it does the only safe thing: it floods the frame out of every port except the one it came in on, exactly like a hub. When the destination answers, the switch learns its port from the answer's source MAC, and from then on traffic to it goes to one port. Broadcast frames are always flooded, because they are meant for every card.

The set of cards that one broadcast reaches is called a broadcast domain. On a normal network that is exactly one IP subnet, the block of addresses that lesson 3 of this track is about. Routers don't forward broadcasts, and that is one reason large networks get split into subnets: with ten thousand hosts in one broadcast domain, every card would spend its time on broadcasts meant for someone else.

Docker's bridge network, which the lab network in this lesson uses, is a software switch inside Docker's Linux virtual machine, and it follows these rules exactly. The Try it shows them from the outside. You listen on a third host, peer, while client talks to router. Peer hears client's broadcast. It doesn't hear the pings that follow, because by then the switch knows which port router is on.

Notice what a switch never reads: IP addresses. It has no idea that ee:02:07:41:4d:8c is 10.10.1.10. That gap is the next section.

try.title: Watch the switch from a third host
steps: From the labs folder, start the lab network: docker compose -f env/net.yml up -d. It has client (10.10.1.10), peer (10.10.1.20) and router (10.10.1.2) on one network called lan, and a server behind the router.

In one terminal, listen on peer: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec peer tcpdump -i eth0 -e -nn 'arp or icmp'. tcpdump prints one line per frame; -e adds the two MAC addresses, -nn shows numbers instead of names, and the filter keeps only ARP and ping traffic.
In a second terminal, run the three commands below: clear client's cache, ping router twice, then ping an address nobody has. Predict first: which of these packets will peer see?
Stop tcpdump with Ctrl-C. Leave the network running for the next two Try its.

code.title: second terminal, in labs/
code.html: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ip neigh flush all docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ping -c 2 10.10.1.2 docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client ping -c 2 10.10.1.99

try.expect:
Peer printed four lines, and not one ping:

17:49:31.128876 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.2 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
17:49:32.189584 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
17:49:33.212002 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
17:49:34.236068 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28

The broadcasts reached peer. Router's reply and all four ICMP packets went only between client and router, so peer never saw them. The who-has for 10.10.1.99 repeats once a second because nobody answers. Your MAC addresses will differ: Docker makes up new ones each time the network starts.

sections.h: ARP asks the whole link who owns an IP address
sections.html:
Here is the gap. Client wants to ping 10.10.1.20. Its routing table, the kernel's list of where to send each range of addresses (lesson 3 of this track), says that address is on its own link, so the frame must carry 10.10.1.20's MAC. Client only knows the IP address. How does it find the MAC?

The simplest answer is a file on every machine that lists each neighbour's IP and MAC. It breaks the first time anything changes. A broken card gets replaced. DHCP, the service that hands out addresses on most networks, gives 10.10.1.20 to a different laptop tomorrow. Docker gives every container a new random MAC each time it starts. Nobody could keep that file correct.

What works is to ask. Client broadcasts one question to every card on the link: "Who has 10.10.1.20? Tell 10.10.1.10." Every machine reads it, and only the owner of 10.10.1.20 answers: "10.10.1.20 is at 4a:9d:40:b1:a5:9e." This is ARP, the Address Resolution Protocol, defined in RFC 826 in 1982 and doing the same job today. ARP isn't carried inside IP. It rides directly in Ethernet frames with EtherType 0x0806, and the whole ARP message is 28 bytes: hardware type 1 (Ethernet), protocol type 0x0800 (IPv4), the two address lengths (6 and 4), an operation (1 for a request, 2 for a reply), then sender MAC, sender IP, target MAC and target IP. In a request the target MAC is all zeros. That empty field is the question.

Three refinements make this cheap.

The reply goes straight back to the asker's MAC, not to everyone. Only the question needs a broadcast.

The asker keeps the answer in its ARP cache, which Linux calls the neighbour table. Without the cache, every packet would cost a broadcast and a round trip before it could leave. With it, a host asks once and then sends straight away.

And the owner learns the asker's MAC from the request itself, because the request carries the sender's IP and MAC. Peer is about to answer client's ping, and thanks to this it can send the reply without asking anything back. RFC 826 states the rule directly: if you are the target, add the sender to your table.

The same RFC has a second rule, for everyone else on the link: a host that already has an entry for the sender refreshes it from any ARP packet it hears, even one aimed at someone else. Hosts that have never met the sender ignore it, so a busy link doesn't fill every cache with strangers. The last section shows what this rule is for.

Step through one exchange, then capture it yourself.

try.title: Capture an ARP exchange
steps: Open a shell on client: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec client bash.
Run the lines below: clear the cache, listen for ARP in the background, send one ping, stop listening and show the cache.
Type exit, then look at peer's cache: docker compose -f env/net.yml exec peer ip neigh show. Predict first: does peer know client's MAC, although peer never asked for it?

code.title: on client
code.html: ip neigh flush all tcpdump -i eth0 -e -nn arp 2>/dev/null & sleep 1; ping -c 1 10.10.1.20 > /dev/null; sleep 1 kill %1 ip neigh show

try.expect:
17:49:49.341213 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.20 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
17:49:49.341243 b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.20 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
17:49:49.341273 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5 > b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Reply 10.10.1.20 is-at 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5, length 28
10.10.1.20 dev eth0 lladdr 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5 REACHABLE

The request went to ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff and the reply came back to client's MAC alone. You will probably see the request twice. Docker turns on hairpin mode on its bridge ports, so the bridge also sends the broadcast back out of the port it came in on, and client's own tcpdump catches the copy. Peer saw it once. Peer's cache shows 10.10.1.10 dev eth0 lladdr b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 DELAY (or STALE): it learned client's MAC from the request, as RFC 826 says.

sections.h: Caches go stale: expiry, probes and announcements
sections.html:
A cache brings back the problem the file had. An answer was true when it arrived, and it can stop being true at any moment: the card gets replaced, a virtual machine moves to another host, an IP address moves to a standby server. A cache that never forgot would keep sending frames to a card that is gone.

The plain fix is to throw entries away after a while and ask again. Linux does that, with one saving. It keeps an entry REACHABLE, meaning trusted, for a random 15 to 45 seconds after it was last confirmed (base_reachable_time_ms is 30,000, and the kernel picks a time between half and one and a half times that). Then the entry turns STALE: still used, but no longer trusted. The next time the kernel sends to a STALE neighbour, the entry goes to DELAY, and if nothing has confirmed the neighbour after 5 seconds, the kernel sends a unicast ARP probe straight to the cached MAC (PROBE). Unicast, because the old answer is probably still right, and asking one card is cheaper than asking all of them. Traffic that proves the neighbour is alive, such as TCP acknowledgments for data you sent, counts as confirmation, so a busy connection rarely needs ARP at all.

Up to 45 seconds plus probes is fine for a replaced laptop. It is far too slow when a database's floating IP, an address that can move between machines, fails over to a standby. So the new owner doesn't wait to be asked. It broadcasts an ARP about its own address: "10.10.1.50 is at my MAC." RFC 5227 calls this an ARP announcement; most people say gratuitous ARP. Every host that was talking to the old machine has an entry for 10.10.1.50, so by RFC 826's refresh rule each of them switches to the new MAC at once. Keepalived, a common Linux tool for floating IPs, sends exactly this when it moves an address.

When nobody answers ARP at all, ping shows it like this (ping uses ICMP, a small control protocol that rides inside IP):

PING 10.10.1.99 (10.10.1.99) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=1 Destination Host Unreachable

Read the From address. It is client's own. No other machine said anything. Client's kernel broadcast three ARP requests a second apart, heard nothing, marked the entry FAILED and dropped the packet. For a destination on your own subnet, Destination Host Unreachable from your own address means no card answered ARP: the host is off, on another network, or using a different address than you think.

The link has one more limit you will run into: frame size. Ethernet carries at most 1,500 bytes of payload per frame, the MTU (maximum transmission unit) from lesson 1. A ping with 1,472 bytes of data, plus 8 bytes of ICMP header and 20 bytes of IP header, fills one frame exactly. Ask for 1,473 with the Don't Fragment flag set and Linux refuses before anything is sent: ping: local error: message too long, mtu=1500. Lesson 4 of this track shows what happens when a router in the middle has a smaller MTU.

try.title: Watch entries age and fail
steps: Open a shell on client again and run the lines below. The sleep 50 gives the entry time to go stale.
Look at the ping to 10.10.1.99: whose address is in From?

In the two MTU pings, -s sets the bytes of data and -M do sets the Don't Fragment flag, which forbids splitting the packet. Predict which one fails, and whether the error comes from peer or from client itself.

On a Mac, arp -an lists the cache (one line per neighbour, without Linux's state names), and ping's Don't Fragment flag is -D: ping -D -s 1472 -c 1 <your gateway> gets an answer, and with -s 1473 no answer comes back.
When you're done, stop the network from the labs folder: docker compose -f env/net.yml down.

code.title: on client
code.html: ip neigh show; sleep 50; ip neigh show ping -c 3 10.10.1.99 ip neigh show 10.10.1.99 ping -M do -s 1472 -c 1 10.10.1.20 ping -M do -s 1473 -c 1 10.10.1.20

try.expect:
From one run (ping statistics trimmed):

10.10.1.20 dev eth0 lladdr 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5 REACHABLE
10.10.1.20 dev eth0 lladdr 3a:42:9a:52:90:f5 STALE

PING 10.10.1.99 (10.10.1.99) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=1 Destination Host Unreachable
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=2 Destination Host Unreachable
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=3 Destination Host Unreachable

--- 10.10.1.99 ping statistics ---
3 packets transmitted, 0 received, +3 errors, 100% packet loss, time 2076ms
10.10.1.99 dev eth0 FAILED

PING 10.10.1.20 (10.10.1.20) 1472(1500) bytes of data.
1480 bytes from 10.10.1.20: icmp_seq=1 ttl=64 time=0.039 ms

PING 10.10.1.20 (10.10.1.20) 1473(1501) bytes of data.
ping: local error: message too long, mtu=1500

The entry went from REACHABLE to STALE while nothing used it. The failed pings report From 10.10.1.10, client itself, and the entry ends up FAILED. The 1,472-byte ping fits one frame exactly; the 1,473-byte one never leaves client, because the kernel knows the link's MTU.

refs.title: Linux kernel docs: IP sysctl (neigh settings)

analogy: ARP is a new employee standing up in an open-plan office and calling out "Who's Priya from settlements? I have a parcel for her." Everyone hears it. Only Priya answers, and she walks over to the newcomer's desk to say "that's me, desk 14", so nobody else has to listen to the answer. She also remembers the newcomer's desk, since she now knows where the call came from. The newcomer writes "Priya, desk 14" on a sticky note, and after a while throws the note away in case she has moved. The analogy breaks on trust: in an office you'd notice if someone else answered to Priya's name. ARP has no such check, and any card on the link can claim any IP address (see Go deeper).
world: This lesson matters most when something moves. Your settlement batch connects to an Oracle database through a floating IP, and the cluster software fails it over to the standby node. The batch hosts that were already talking to the database have an ARP entry pointing at the old node's MAC. If the new node announces the IP with a gratuitous ARP, every one of those hosts switches within a millisecond. If the announcement is lost or blocked, they keep sending frames to a machine that no longer answers for that IP, until the entry goes stale and a probe fails, which can take tens of seconds, and your JDBC pool reports timeouts rather than connection errors. In a cloud VPC (your private network inside AWS or another cloud) there is no shared broadcast link at all: the provider's network answers ARP itself, which is why floating IPs there move through an API call instead of a gratuitous ARP. You meet ARP failures on bare metal, virtual machines and on-premises clusters, which is where many payment databases still live.
mistake: The common mistake is reading Destination Host Unreachable as "the server is down" or "a firewall blocked me". When the From address is your own, nothing on the network said anything: your kernel never got an ARP reply. Usually the host is down, but just as often the address or the subnet mask is wrong, so your machine thinks a remote host is on its own link and ARPs for it, or the two hosts are plugged into different networks. Check ip route get <ip> (is there a via?), ip neigh show <ip> (FAILED or INCOMPLETE?) and the other host's ip addr before you open a ticket.

steps.say: A reconciliation job on client can't reach a service at 10.10.1.99. Ping gives the first clue: the errors come From 10.10.1.10, client's own address. So no other machine answered at all.
steps.code:
$ ping -c 3 10.10.1.99
PING 10.10.1.99 (10.10.1.99) 56(84) bytes of data.
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=1 Destination Host Unreachable
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=2 Destination Host Unreachable
From 10.10.1.10 icmp_seq=3 Destination Host Unreachable

steps.say: Ask the kernel how it would send to that address. There is no via, so it thinks 10.10.1.99 is on its own link and ARPs for the host itself. Compare an address on the other subnet, which goes via the router.
steps.code:
$ ip route get 10.10.1.99
10.10.1.99 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.10 uid 0
    cache
$ ip route get 10.10.2.99
10.10.2.99 via 10.10.1.2 dev eth0 src 10.10.1.10 uid 0
    cache

steps.say: Look at the neighbour entry. FAILED means the kernel asked and nobody answered.
steps.code:
$ ip neigh show 10.10.1.99
10.10.1.99 dev eth0 FAILED

steps.say: Watch the wire to be sure. Three broadcasts a second apart, and no reply. Peer, listening on the same switch, saw exactly these.
steps.code:
b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28
b2:34:8a:ab:b5:24 > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff, ethertype ARP (0x0806), length 42: Request who-has 10.10.1.99 tell 10.10.1.10, length 28

steps.say: The problem is on the link, not in routing and not in the service. Either 10.10.1.99 is down, or it isn't on this network, or it has a different address. Check its ip addr and which network it is attached to. If the route had shown via 10.10.1.2, the ARP would have been for the router, and the same error would mean the router itself wasn't answering.

lab.title: Build an ARP cache that follows RFC 826
steps: Run the tests once from the labs folder. All 16 fail. Two of them decode the real request and reply from the Try it, stored in src/test/resources/sfz/net/l02/.
In MacAddress.kt, write isBroadcast, isMulticast and isLocallyAdministered. Each is one line on bits or firstOctet.
In ArpPacket.kt, write decode as the mirror image of encode, which is already written. Check the hardware type, protocol type and both lengths first.
In ArpCache.kt, write lookup with its time limit, then receive. Follow the four numbered rules in its comment, in order: the order is what RFC 826 specifies.
Run the tests until all 16 pass, then read the ArpCacheTest test names in order. Together they are RFC 826's reception rules.
hints: firstOctet and 0x01 != 0 means (firstOctet and 0x01) != 0: in Kotlin, named infix functions like and bind tighter than !=.
MacAddress.of(bytes, 8) and ipv4FromBytes(bytes, 14) read the sender's addresses. The target's start at 18 and 24.
In receive, check the table with table[packet.senderIp], not with lookup(): an entry older than the TTL still counts as being in the table, and still gets refreshed.
The reply swaps roles. You are the sender (myMac, myIp), and the asker's MAC and IP go into the target fields.
A test fails with an entry that is 30 s old? lookup must reject it when clock() - updatedAt is equal to the TTL, not only when it is greater.

drill.title: Write the exchange from memory
drill.prompt: Host A (10.10.1.10, MAC aa:..) pings host B (10.10.1.20, MAC bb:..) on the same switch. All caches are empty. Write every frame until the first ping leaves, with its Ethernet destination and its ARP fields, and what each host's cache holds after each frame. Then check the answer.

answer.html:
1. aa:.. > ff:ff:ff:ff:ff:ff   ARP request: who-has 10.10.1.20 tell 10.10.1.10
   ARP fields: sender aa:.. / 10.10.1.10, target 00:00:00:00:00:00 / 10.10.1.20
   switch: learns aa:.. is on A's port, floods the frame to every other port
   A: empty, packet waiting    B: 10.10.1.10 at aa:.. (learned from the request)
   other hosts: ignore it, unless they already had an entry for 10.10.1.10

2. bb:.. > aa:..   ARP reply: 10.10.1.20 is-at bb:..
   ARP fields: sender bb:.. / 10.10.1.20, target aa:.. / 10.10.1.10
   switch: learns bb:.., sends the frame to A's port only
   A: 10.10.1.20 at bb:.. REACHABLE

3. aa:.. > bb:..   IPv4 10.10.1.10 > 10.10.1.20 ICMP echo request (no more ARP)

recap: A MAC address is 48 bits for one card on one link. The lowest bit of the first byte marks group addresses; the next bit marks made-up ones, like Docker's.
A switch learns source MACs per port, sends known unicast out of one port, and floods broadcasts and unknown destinations. It never reads IP addresses.
ARP fills that gap: a broadcast who-has, a unicast is-at. The target learns the asker from the request, and hosts that know the sender refresh their entry from anything it sends.
Linux neighbour entries go REACHABLE, STALE, DELAY, PROBE, and FAILED when nobody answers. Forgetting is deliberate, so a replaced machine gets found again.
Destination Host Unreachable from your own address on your own subnet means ARP got no answer.
Ethernet's MTU is 1,500 bytes: 1,472 bytes of ping data plus 28 bytes of headers fill one frame.

explain.prompt: A teammate asks how the very first packet from their service to a new host on the same subnet gets the right MAC address, and why that first packet is sometimes slower than the rest. Explain it.
explain.answer: The kernel needs the destination MAC for the Ethernet header, and the switch can't help because it only knows MACs, not IPs. So the kernel holds the packet and broadcasts an ARP request: who has 10.10.1.20, tell 10.10.1.10. Every host on the subnet gets it, and only the owner of 10.10.1.20 answers, with a reply sent straight back to our MAC. The owner also keeps our MAC from the request, so it can answer without asking. Our kernel caches the answer and sends the packet it was holding. That exchange is an extra round trip on the LAN, usually far under a millisecond, but if a request is lost the kernel waits a second before trying again. Later packets use the cache until the entry goes stale, and then the kernel checks with a unicast probe, not another broadcast.

deeper.html:
ARP spoofing. ARP has no authentication. Any card on the link can send a reply claiming to be the gateway, and RFC 826's refresh rule means every host that already knows the gateway will believe it and start sending its traffic to the liar. That is ARP spoofing, the classic way to sit in the middle of a LAN. Switches can defend against it (Dynamic ARP Inspection checks replies against what DHCP handed out), and so can the layers above: with TLS, a machine in the middle sees only ciphertext. It is one more reason payment traffic is encrypted inside the data centre too.

VLANs. A VLAN splits one physical switch into several broadcast domains. The switch adds a 4-byte 802.1Q tag after the source MAC (EtherType 0x8100) carrying a 12-bit VLAN ID, and only floods within the same VLAN. Hosts usually never see the tag, because the switch adds and removes it at the edge. Each VLAN is normally one IP subnet, which is why "wrong VLAN" and "wrong subnet" produce the same ARP failure.

IPv6 has no ARP. It uses Neighbor Discovery, which sends a neighbour solicitation to a multicast group derived from the target address, so only a few cards have to look at it. ip -6 neigh shows the table on Linux and ndp -an on a Mac. Lesson 5 of this track covers it.

Wi-Fi looks like Ethernet to your kernel. An 802.11 frame carries three or four MAC addresses, including the access point's, but the Wi-Fi driver converts frames to Ethernet form, so your laptop's kernel, ARP and tcpdump see ordinary Ethernet on en0.
